utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. So now for the record, all the accused are here. I notice some absentees amongst the Defence teams; Mr. Nikolic for the Beara Defence team; Mr. Bourgon for the Nikolic team; Mr. Lazarevic for the Borovcanin Defence team; Mr. Krgovic for the Gvero Defence team. That's it. Prosecution today is like last week, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell. Yes. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I think for the next couple of days, at least, that will remain the position. Hopefully in the course of the week, Judge Stole will be able to join us, probably either Wednesday or Thursday. Mr. McCloskey, last week we asked our senior legal officer to approach you to state in court if now you know the whereabouts of Mr. Jasikovic, Jasikovac. My apologies. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The answer is yes, we think we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need it in open session. If that is the case -- yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be coming down very, very soon with our decision on the Gvero motions on a number of exhibits. However, you will recall that in the course of the testimony of Mr. Jevdjevic and General Kosovac, there were some exhibits tendered which remain the subject matter of an objection by some of you. These are not, strictly speaking, covered by the two Gvero motions that we will be deciding. I would very much like to know if you've had time to sit down around the table together and discuss the contested exhibits. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, not yet. I was asked about this on Friday, I believe, and we've been trying to sort out which ones of those exhibits are contested, and we should be able to meet today since everyone is here now, and I'm not sure there's -- we don't have a record of a lot of contested exhibits aside from the ones in the motion, but we'll sort that out with everyone hopefully this afternoon. I don't see any reason why we can't sort it out this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for our part, I hoped I made clear on the 2nd of March that I had come to an agreement with Mr. Vanderpuye, in fact, on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, about two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: About two documents, yes. It's 4208, which is going to be admitted, and 4220, which is not going to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's the agreement. In other words, you would also agree that the last of these two documents, the latter be not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But does that exhaust the problems or the issues raised by you in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm bound to say I thought so in as much as the objections were meant to cover only such matters or such documents as we were in fact objecting to. It was Mr. Vanderpuye who wanted me to make it clear that we were not objecting to P4208. I had hoped that was implicit by the fact it wasn't it objections motion, but I welcome the opportunity to speak to Mr. McCloskey and confirm the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked you because last week, as you can well imagine now, we were discussing this with our staff, and the impression was that the objections were not limited to these two documents only, so I was acting under that assumption, but I would be happy to know that I was wrong or that my staff was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I suspect I'm the cause of the misunderstanding. Let me try and resolve it in the next few hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that so much, Mr. Josse. Thank you. Yes. I think we can start now unless there are other preliminaries you would like to raise? Yes. The other thing is this, Mr. McCloskey, the Besina witnesses that you wanted to call, do you know the timing of them roughly? Because I got information through our senior legal officer that the lacuna that the Pandurevic Defence team was expecting to encounter in the course of the week, particularly Wednesday and also for awhile tomorrow, were going to be filled in by you, by the Prosecution. I don't have information whether that applies, also, to today, and what's the programme going to be like, the schedule going to be like for the rest of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding is that we have one witness that's here that should be ready to go tomorrow sometime, if we reach that point, and -- yeah, that -- I can go into private session. I'm not sure. I think we had filed a motion for protective measures on this witness. So we should have someone that's here in time as far as I know. I haven't heard the latest on travel arrangements, but the plan was the person was here and could be ready to testify when they ran out of witnesses, which was going to be expected tomorrow sometime, I think, unless, you know, we do sometimes what we do and keep them. The other witness was coming on Tuesday night, which means we won't really have a chance to talk to them until Wednesday morning, and so Wednesday, it appears Wednesday morning is a down day, and we thought we could either start at 10.30 or we could perhaps see if the afternoon court would change with us, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is acceptable -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We do have a problem with Wednesday afternoon, so your suggestion to start the sitting later in the morning of Wednesday would be acceptable. So Wednesday we will start at 10.30 rather than 9.00. Okay. Instead of 9.00. Yes. Thank you. Now, no preliminaries? Right. So we have a leftover from General Pandurevic's testimony. That is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we have all agreed we will deal with the witness first and deal with the tendering afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't know that. All right. You don't seem convinced, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are ready to do that a little later. We spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. God help everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are most welcome. You have been summoned by General Pandurevic as one of his witnesses. Before you start your testimony, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth and the whole truth. Madam usher is going to hand you the text of the declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You will be asked some questions by counsel for General Pandurevic, Mr. Sarapa, who will introduce himself better to you. And afterwards, you will be asked some questions possibly on cross-examination. Mr. Sarapa, please go ahead. Examination by by Mr. Sarapa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning. God help you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the records I have to introduce myself, although you know me. My same is Djordje Sarapa, and I'm Defence counsel for Vinko Pandurevic. Could you please introduce yourself and give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Zvonko Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: 6th September, 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we are speaking the same language, before you answer my question, could you please look at the screen in front of you and see if the typing has finished, because that's the English translation, and we want to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you finish primary school?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you completed the secondary school and which school?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina and Tuzla, the trade of auto mechanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do the compulsory military service in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which places?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In 1972 over 1973 in Kraljevo and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which army -- in which arm of the service did you do your service?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The auto unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm unemployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war, before the war broke out in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what was your occupation or occupations from when you first began to work until the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was a haulier. I worked in catering, and just before the war I worked as a commercial manager in a private company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you mobilised into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which units, in what positions were you during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised into the technical service, the procurement section, the Vlasenica Battalion. Later --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the summer of 1992, I was assigned to the Birac Brigade to the same job, the technical service procurement clerk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have a rank, but I should probably mention that when the Drina Corps was established, I was moved from the brigade into the Drina Corps, into the logistics, also to serve as a procurement desk officer, without a rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you demobed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I think in July 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a rank at the time when you were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I had been given the rank of 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, do you remember telling -- or, rather, giving a statement to the Pandurevic Defence team certified by a notary public?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion, or, rather, have you had an occasion since you arrived in The Hague to see that statement again and peruse it again?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday evening you showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that statement the true reflection of what you actually stated?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, if you were asked the same questions today, would you answer the question the same way as you did at the moment when you were providing the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for you, sir. I would like to read the summary of the witness's statement at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In July 1995, the witness was a member of the technical service in the command of the Drina Corps. He was a desk officer. His rank was 2nd lieutenant. He performed the duties of procurement, logistics, and he procured technical equipment for the staff command of the Drina Corps. On the 11th of July, 1995, the witness brought to the command of the Bratunac Brigade food that had been prepared elsewhere. It was fish, carp. The food was brought to be served as dinner to the officers of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, of the Drina Corps, and the brigades. That happened late in the evening. The persons who were present were as follows: General Ratko Mladic, General Radislav Krstic, and other officers. The witness remembers that Vinko Pandurevic was also there. He has known Vinko Pandurevic since 1993. The officers came for dinner after a meeting that had been held at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. The witness also remembers that on that day, the Army of Republika Srpska had entered Srebrenica. The witness is certain that this happened on the 11th of July because that was the eve of the day of St. Peter. St. Peter's Day is a church holiday which the Serb orthodox church celebrates on 12 July. Since the dinner was served on the 11th of July, which was part of the feast of the fast of St. Peter, fish had to be served as part of that fast. On the following day, the 12th of July, there was a celebration of St. Peter's Day in Vlasenica. St. Peter's Day is the day of the church in Vlasenica. The church is actually dedicated to the apostles Peter and Paul, and the witness is the godfather of the church in Vlasenica. On St. Peter's Day, i.e., on the 12th of July, the witness hosted lunch at the Panorama Hotel in Vlasenica. St. Peter's Day is also the day of the municipality and the town of Vlasenica, and this brings the summary statement to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender document number 7D1092, which is the witness's statement provided on the 27th of December, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Any objections other members of the Defence teams? Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's so admitted. Do you have any further questions to the witness, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I have just two more questions for you. Can you please tell us, why did you bring food to the Bratunac Brigade that evening? Was that of your own initiative, or had somebody asked you to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, I prepared food for the evening. It was a meat-free meal, and at the same time we prepared meat for the following day, for the holiday celebration that would take place on the 12th of July. 12th of July is the day when we celebrate the two apostles, St. Peter and St. Paul. Sometime in the afternoon hours, I believe that it was around 1700 hours, Colonel Acamovic called me. He was the assistant commander for logistics in the Drina Corps. He asked me whether I would be able to allocate some of the food that was being prepared for the evening meal on the 11th of July to be served to the guests who would be attending dinner and who were supposed to arrive from Serbia and Montenegro and from some regions of what is today Republika Srpska. He asked me to take that food to Bratunac because General Mladic was in Bratunac, and also General Krstic was there, and some ten or so officers together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you can go a bit faster.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I said I could certainly do that, but that I couldn't do it before half past 8.00. I cannot leave for Bratunac before half past 8.00. He said, Very well, deal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you told? Where were you supposed to take that food for dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: To the command of the Bratunac Brigade, which was located in the fabric -- in the factory of ceramic tiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one part in your previous answer. You mentioned guests from Serbia and Montenegro who had been invited. What did Acamovic tell you? Who were you supposed to bring the food for? Could you please be more precise in your answer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: For General Mladic, General Krstic, and some ten or so other officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, had you ever prepared food for reputable guests before that evening?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, a number of times. There were many such occasions, and yours truly was honoured by having hosted in my own house the patriarch of Moscow and entire Russia. His name is Pemin, and he was retired from his duties maybe a month ago. Very often I hosted our own patriarch, Pavle, as he would be passing through our region, and he would always pay me a visit no matter who he was accompanied with. I would also like to point out that I served as a host before the war to the Mufti of Belgrade and entire Serbia, Mr. Jusufspahic - I believe that is his name - and that happened every time when he was on his way to Sarajevo and on his way back when he was headed for meetings with reis-ul-ulema. He trusted that the food that I would prepare for him would be prepared according to the rules of Koran. I also had an occasion to play host in my own house to the former president of America, Mr. Jimmy Carter, who was on a state visit to President Karadzic. Two members of his delegation also spent the night in my house that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Bajagic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Now, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No question for the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was told this morning you had anticipated an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it some strange Monday feeling or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. I wanted to ask for 15 minutes to consult, but, you know, I think that we can pass at this point. If something comes up, I'll sure address to the Court, and I'll leave it to your discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Happy to join the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Mitchell, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Remember that he is unemployed, so instead of a cross-examination, perhaps you could offer him a job as a chef for the Office of the Prosecution. I'm sure he will keep you all happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: God be with you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, if at any point when I'm asking you questions I look down, I'm not being rude. I'm just checking that the transcript is coming through correctly. I'd like to start off and ask you some questions about your relationship with Mr. Pandurevic. When did you first meet Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: We met at the Main Staff. I think, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how often did you see him in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Not very often, no. I saw him from time to time when he was appointed as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, but I don't know when that happened. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How would you describe your relationship with him? Was it purely professional, or did you regard him as a friend?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not a professional soldier, so our relationship could not have been a professional relationship. I liked the man at the time because he hailed from the same region. He hailed from the Romanija plateau just as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw him, I found him a bit strange, a bit odd. I looked at him to see who he reminded me of because people looking like him are very few and far between in the region where we come from. There are big and strong men like him, but there are no ginger and freckled people like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you know Milenko Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: He arrived at the command of the Drina Corps when he was appointed as a signalsman, and that's when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How would you describe your relationship with Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Jevdjevic is a poet, and I am a fiddler, so we made a good team. He wrote poetry, and I sang his poetry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you were friends with Mr. Jevdjevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say friends. We socialised, yes. There is a difference between just a mate and a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you still socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall the last time you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting of poets somewhere. I don't even remember where. He passed by my house, and he stopped to say hello. I don't know when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you recall even the year?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you know Sreten Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. The name doesn't ring a bell. Can you jog my memory, maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The assistant commander for logistics in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Miladin Mijatovic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Zlotovic"] from the Zvornik Brigade, logistics organ?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: And what period of time are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Between 1992 to 1995, during the war.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't socialise with him. He lives in Zvornik, I live in Vlasenica. The distance between the two is about 50 kilometres, and I don't know why I would socialise with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you would have spoken to him regularly as part of your work in the logistics organ; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake in the transcript in line 12 on this page. It says Miladin Zlotovic. Could the Prosecutor be asked to repeat the family name of the person so that it may be recorded properly, because the person's name is not Zlotovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Miladin Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Bajagic, when you said I know him, yes, you were actually referring to Miladin Mijatovic and not to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mijatovic. If that's the person you are asking me about, then I know who you are talking about, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just confirming with you. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you would have spoken with Mr. Mijatovic regularly as part of your work in the Drina Corps logistics organ; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. There was nothing to talk about. He was a logistics man. As far as I know, he was with the Zvornik Brigade and I was with the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So isn't it --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: We had our superiors. I don't know what you think that we were talking about. We did speak about bees, honey, and mushrooms, about medicinal herbs because that was his particular hobby, and it still is. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you've told us about -- you mentioned Lazar Acamovic the assistant commander for rear services. What was your relationship with him like?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, our relationship was a relationship between a subordinate and a superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what about Rajko Krsmanovic? How was your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The name doesn't ring a bell. Who is Rajko Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Head of transportation service in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it was nothing special. We were very official in our everyday business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, as a member of the Drina Corps, you must have known Vujadin Popovic; correct.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you're a logistics man. Do you recall what kind of car Mr. Popovic drove?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So do you know any of the other accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I know General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, he was assistant commander for moral guidance and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you socialise with General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: What? Well, to tell you the truth, it was a bit weird to me that a general and a communist should be appointed assistant commander for religious [Realtime transcript read in error, "logistics"] affairs, but I could see that he was a good man, a good person. And since I am president of the church union in my hometown for almost 35 years now, and I was twice president of the management board in the parish of Tuzla and Zvornik, and there was a drive at the time to achieve a reapportionment between the the church and the army and the military leadership, so on that level we had certain contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one error in translation. This is page 19, line 1. Instead logistics, he said religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I'd like to talk to you about when you first joined the VRS in April of 1992. Your statement says that you were drafted; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So were you ordered to join the army, or did you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was a mobilisation drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you were ordered?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I abide by the mobilisation. If I had not responded, I don't know, but there would have been certain sanctions, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, prior to that in 1991, you were involved in arming the Serbs in the Vlasenica area in their defence against the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Serb civilians and the Territorial Defence started arming themselves in the Vlasenica area in 1991, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they started arming, but I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could we please go to 65 ter 4412. I have a hard copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is an intercepted conversation dated 11 December 1991 between you and Radovan Karadzic. I'd just like to read some of the first page. It starts off with: You: "Koljevic? "Yes? "Mr. Koljevic, it's Bajagic from Vlasenica. "Oh, how are you doing? "Well, fine." And Radovan Karadzic comes on: "... Zvonko. "With God's help, and how are you? "May God help you. How are you? "Well, fine. I can hear that you are busy. I'll make it short. "Yes, yes, we have some foreign journalists here. "Well, we are, perhaps you know it, Rajko told you, now before, this now, the plebiscite, when we had rallies, offered mobilisation, voluntary, army to the people. "Yes. "And the response we had, it's simply amazing! About 600 volunteers in two days."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic says: "Brilliant." And then you say: "They have all been clothed and armed." Sir, this is you talking about armed volunteers in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I said they were clothed and armed because it was a mobilisation drive. The Yugoslav Army was there at the time. They organised the mobilisation, and it was mostly Serbs who responded to the call-up. There were some Muslims who did so too. It was the Yugoslav Army that provided the equipment and the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in English. If we go down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You say: "We'll bring trumpet players from Uzice, a military orchestra from Sarajevo. "I see. And somebody will ... here, our commander has left to see if he can get General Durdevac to support. "Yes, I see. "And seeing that the party has done it all, the job and the bauxite mine ... will be nice if someone can come and be there tomorrow. "I tell you what, I think that the party should ... what is being done there is great, but now it's finished, and people have been clothed, to avoid the army together accused of being affiliated to a party, I mean, it wouldn't be a good idea for ... "For somebody to come?" "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's page 2. It should be on the screen in front of you as well.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: All right. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, this isn't the JNA arming these people, is it? It's the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA, if they drafted him, they will give him weapons, not a shovel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, we see you saying: "And seeing that the party has done it all ..." That's the SDS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't mean the SDS. What did the party do? Tell me where. Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's close to the bottom of the second page. It's the sixth box from the bottom, your name, and it says: "And seeing that the party has done it all, the job and the bauxite mine, it will be nice if someone could come and be there tomorrow." So is the reference to the party, is that a reference to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a member of the party and we organised ourselves to prepare that a lunch for the troops to the best of our ability and to get the bauxite mine to help with organising the lunch and the celebration and the feast, to bring the music, the wheel dance, et cetera, the singing. We got involved to organise that part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when you say you were a member of the party, you were a member of the SDS party; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the SDS, but to me this is a popular movement, a movement of the people. I was never a member of the political party, and I don't accept that. 90 per cent of the Serbs were in that movement in 1991 until it all started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, that answer is not very clear. Were you or were you not a member of the SDS in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was part of the SDS, but I accepted that SDS as a movement for the salvation of the Serbian people, not politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how long were you a member of the SDS party for?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Until -- I don't know which year, maybe 2002, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to another topic. I'd like to talk about your promotion during the war. You told us that you joined the army as a private; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you left the army as a 2nd lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As a 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall in 1993 that General Zivanovic recommended that you be promoted from private to captain 1st class?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: 1993? I don't know, maybe. Well, how can you be promoted straight from a private to a captain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we please look at 65 ter 4410.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Promotion from a private to a captain 1st class is a big jump, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Oh, I wish. I wish, because where I live, captains are much more popular than colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at this order or this recommendation for Zvonko Bajagic, private, recommendation for exceptional promotion. If we go down, he is recommending that you be promoted to the rank of reserves captain 1st class at the technical services, and we see your name. If we can go to the next page of the document in English, and I'd just like to read out some of this explanation to you: "Since the first days of the battle of the Serbian people, the above named has engaged himself to the utmost as well as his family, relatives, and friends, selflessly dedicating himself to materially equipping the Serbian soldiers and units. Since the day of the formation of the corps, he has been put in a very responsible position, which he maintains very successfully. As is the nature of this work to handle goods of high material" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: "... a person of weaker morals would succumb to temptation; however, we may proudly state that Zvonko is a truly honourable Serb, whose decency honouring orthodoxy manifests the guiding star towards the salvation and victory of the Serbian people. All those sincerely wishing well to the Serbian people can regard an ideal in the character of Zvonko Bajagic. This command recommends to the Superior Command to promote the above named to the rank of reserve's captain 1st class of the Army of Republika Srpska. The rank we are recommending will be given to a man who will never and nowhere underestimate or belittle it." And this goes to the organ for personnel matters of the Main Staff. Sir, do you know why General Zivanovic proposed this exceptional promotion in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I would like to get this to leave it to my grandchildren for my family archives. I'm really proud to have something as nice as this written about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, do you recall why General Zivanovic proposed that you be promoted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's beginning to come back to me now. Being in the corps command and in that service for procurement, serving as a desk officer for procurement, it had to be someone with a rank, whereas I was a private, so maybe it was a requirement of the personnel department that I be given a rank, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to suggest to you that while your military position may have been just a clerk in the Drina Corps logistics organ, you were actually a very wealthy, influential man in Vlasenica at the time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends what you call wealthy. Define wealthy. I was wealthy in spirit first. I was one of the well-off people in my area, having created all I had with my own hands, praying to God all the time, and I never worked for a state-run company. I always worked in private business. I was always self-employed, and that was always the thorn in the side of the Yugoslav authorities. Private initiative and entrepreneurship was not allowed to develop, but I did as I did. And as for influential, I wouldn't call it influential. Influential would be something else. I was a prominent head of household in my parish, and that reputation was well earned among the Serbs and the Muslims by my loyalty and faith and honourable work. In my business, I never cheated anyone. I never owed money to anyone. If I wasn't able to help a person, I did not do them any harm either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You were entrusted with some very important work in the Drina Corps, weren't you, sir? You used to deal with important issues such as the procurement of fuel from Serbia for the use of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You say important work. Other people did it before me, but when materiel and equipment had to be collected from somewhere, taken over, I always really only collected, whereas the people who did that job before me, collected something and brought it, it turned out that something was always missing. As for myself, whatever I brought back, nothing was ever missing, and that was well respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, did you used to talk to General Mladic and General Perisic about the procurement of this fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I did talk to them on friendly terms as a host, nothing to do with the affairs of the Main Staff and the military leadership. I mean, who was I to talk to them about such things? Perisic called on me sometimes at my home, visited, if that means anything. But the fact that everybody visited, I can tell you it's explained by the fact that everybody was curious to see the inside of my house. I can tell you that you won't find a house anything like mine in all of Republika Srpska or in Montenegro or in perhaps Serbia. My house is more than a museum. It has so many artifacts and exhibits of the history of Serbs, that maybe not even the museum in Cetinje can boast that much. I even have the remains of Archdeacon Stephane, one of Christ's martyrs, and the way I live is practically the same way of living that was practiced by St. Sava. We always pray before meals, we respect God, we make toasts regularly, and this house protocol, which is the church protocol, was always well respected where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think it's time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Time for a break. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you about you dealing with important issues such as the procurement of fuel from Serbia. There were occasions where you donated fuel personally to the VRS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You said the army of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: To the VRS. You donated fuel to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, not me. How could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You also met regularly with President Karadzic in 1994 and 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Not in 1994, but in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So not in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You met with him regularly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say regularly. We met in 1991 at pre-election rallies, and then in the course of the war, sometimes he would pop over to my house, sometimes I would visit him in Pale. That's how often we met. Those were our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll look at that more closely in a minute. I'd just like to go back to this -- what you said at page 26 when I asked you did you talk to General Mladic and General Perisic about the procurement of fuel, and you said: "Well, I did talk to them on friendly terms as a host, nothing to do with the ... Main Staff and the military leadership. I mean, who was I to talk to them about such things?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So if we can have a look at 65 ter 4416, page 2 in the English, page 1 in the B/C/S. I have a hard copy for the witness. Perhaps I can just hand it straight it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is a conversation dated the 21st of April, 1995, 1955 hours, and it's between General Zivanovic and Zvonko Bajagic. I'd just like to read out the first part of this intercept: Zvonko, how are you? "Don't ask. "What is it? "What can I tell you, not even Mladic was able do anything today. "Why, what happened? The cargo did not go through? "Right. "O, boy, what will happen now? "I have almost gone crazy. "So, nobody can transport it now? "Well, Mladic cannot, and neither can Perisic, I spoke to them three times today. "Yes. "Mladic called from our place, but that papa did not give a green light. They have been been avoiding all contact, and we could see what was going on. "Is there any hope? "There is hope, but they said after Sunday, and since it cannot go through right now, we brought it all back. "Of course, and did you right bringing it back; you wouldn't want it to go to ruin, do you. "It was very awkward, and I'm having a hard time with this, I feel sick. "All right. We will talk later, I understand everything, it is clear to me." So in this intercept, you said that you spoke with Mladic and Perisic three times that day; correct? Let me take a step back. Do you recall this conversation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you doubt that this intercept is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can say that it may have happened that I went and take over some of the materiel and equipment, and then those could not be transported across the Drina, and since Perisic came to my house, we socialised and we were on first-term basis. I may have called him; I may have told him, Why did you give it to us if you don't allow us to take it over the border? That may have been the gist of that conversation, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you were talking to General Mladic and General Perisic about bringing cargo in across the border?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I may have spoken to him about that cargo. Maybe they did not allow the cargo to go through. Maybe that's why I called him to help me have the cargo go through. That may well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall what this cargo was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that, and it doesn't say here. There are all sorts of cargos. I don't know which cargo is this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at 65 ter 4417.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a nickname during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Duga Puska. Translation: Long Rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, so this an intercept dated the 7th of June, 1995, at 1005 hours between Zvonko Bajagic, aka Puska, from the Drina Corps Command in Vlasenica and a certain Misko from Valjevo. So do you know who Misko from Valjevo is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall the name Mitar Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: If you could jog my memory if you know who he is. Could you please jog my memory? I can't remember who that person is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since he suggested this, you can put a direct question, a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, our information is that Mitar Lazarevic was involved with a transport company in Serbia in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at the first part of this intercept. I'm not going to read it all out, but we can see here that you are organising to get 10 tonnes of petrol from Beopetrol in Belgrade, and it's to come across the border before 2 a.m. that night. Do you recall this transaction?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several such transactions. I can't remember the one that you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And see here you say: "Tonight. "How should the man return? "Nothing. He will be escorted, and he will cross it tonight and return tomorrow. And M says something that wasn't picked up. And: "It doesn't matter. It's not a problem. It has been agreed upon at an upper level 01-01." Who is 01?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: 01 was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You were saying 01 to 01. So who is General Mladic talking to?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Probably 01 is probably Perisic. Gvero was 04.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, we are seeing documents in this case from the Drina Corps 5th Engineering Battalion for the pontoon company, he's organising ferry crossing points across the Drina river, at Samsko, Fakovici, Patricia [phoen] and Sapotnik. Do you know what came across at those ferry points?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: When I went to take over different means and equipment in Serbia, I never brought anything across the pontoon bridges. I don't know anything about them or where they were. I transported everything across the regular bridges, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. One more intercept on this topic, 65 ter 411. That's page 3 in the English, page 2 in the B/C/S, just down at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is an intercept dated the 8th of June, 1995, so the next day. If you can just take a moment and read through it. Let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to read from here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page as well. What we can see is only four lines of a conversation between Basevic and Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm reading here is not my dialect, if I can comment upon this. Well, I see on the second page, this is not my dialect. This is not the way I speak. These are not my words. I did not utter this. This was uttered by some Serbians who say "brej" [phoen] which I never would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you doubt the accuracy of this intercept or the authenticity of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, there are three on that page. Which one is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The intercept we're talking about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one we see on the screen now, in other words? That's the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It started off at page 2 in the B/C/S and went over onto page 3. It's the only one with his name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't actually recall the witness being directed to any particular intercept. On page 2, there were three separate intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He's got a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Tell him to read the bottom of page 2 over to page 3 and then ask him for his comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the first page, what I mean is page 2 where the intercept starts. So, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's the intercept down the bottom of the second page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which starts at the bottom in both languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct, and then goes on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, it might be more helpful if you just look at the screen instead of the hard copy. Now, is this the intercept that you said you didn't think was your dialect?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It's not me. I use different words. I use a different dialect. I don't use the words that I read here. I can see the word "cretin," which is not part of my vocabulary. What I did was honest, was lawful. I never smuggled any cigars or cigarettes like I can read here. Those were some thiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, what about the first intercept that we talked about this morning, the one from 1991 between you and Radovan Karadzic. Was that you on that intercept?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we were talking about the lunch that had to be prepared before the lining up of the battalion in Milici; is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's right. That was you on that intercept? Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to something else you said just after the break, and I asked you: "There were occasions where you donated fuel personally to the VRS ..." And you said: "No, not me. How could I?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can look at 65 ter 4415.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That is Drina Corps report dated 29 November 1994, listing the amounts of fuel received from municipalities, enterprises, and donators in the period from the 1st of September to the 15th of November, 1994. If we can go over to the second page. About halfway down the page, we see your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can blow that up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you see your name there, sir? It's 1, 2, 3, 4 from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And it says that in October 1994, Zvonko Bajagic from Vlasenica donated 8.270 litres of D2 diesel and 14.690 litres of petrol to the Drina Corps. So how did your name end up on this document as a donator of fuel to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been some company or some private persons who donated that, and maybe I took the quantities over and brought them back, but it's really beyond my comprehension that you could think that I was in a position to donate those quantities of fuel to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So this document which went to the Main Staff is mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: A hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have one other thing I'd like to ask you about before we get to 1995. Now, sir, you said -- I asked you whether you met regularly with President Karadzic, and you said sometimes he would pop over to your house, sometimes you would visit him in Pale. "That's how often we met. Those were our meetings." Whereabouts in Pale did you meet?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in his office, sometime in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of how often? Once a month, once every six months?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was not very often, from time to time; it all depended. When he needed to see me or wanted to see me, he would call me and he would say, Can you come over, have lunch or dinner. That's what it all boiled down to. It was not that often. There were some official visits regarding the civilian authorities in Vlasenica, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can look at 65 ter 4413. If we can go to page 25 in the B/C/S and page 16 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is President Karadzic's appointment diary from 1994, which was picked up during his arrest last year. Now, this is the entry for the 25th of February, 1994, and the fourth name down is Zvonko Bajagic. That's you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, and yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to page 18 in the English, page 29 in the B/C/S. If we can scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see your name again there, can't we, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you met with President Karadzic on these two dates; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember either the days or the times. It may have happened this way. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...interview the secretaries, and they say that that plus sign is an indication that you came. So you must have met with the president on those days; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's recorded in his notebook, then I must have been there, but I can't remember. It was such a long time ago. I don't have the recollection of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, if we went through this diary page by page, your name would be there I believe 18 times. That's an average of more than once a month, isn't it? We're talking just about 1994 here.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: What are you saying? I don't know. It's nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'm saying that you met with President Karadzic 18 times in 1994, and that's an average of more than once a month, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: If that's what it says in there, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So how is it that a clerk from the Drina Corps logistics organ is meeting with the president that regularly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I told you that I met Radovan the first time in 1991, during the election campaign at rallies. My great grandfather, late Bozo Bajagic, who was actually not my grandfather but my grandfather's first cousin, was living in Niksic and was neighbours with late Vuko Bajagic [as interpreted], Radovan Karadzic's father. They were very good friends. And when I went to Niksic as a child and as a student or a teenager, as the popular word has it nowadays, I really liked to go to Vuk's house with my late grandfather Bozo, and I would listen to them speaking in a very nice way, and I particularly liked listening to Radovan's late mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: May I finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I did not know Radovan. I just knew he was Vuko's son. I mean, I didn't know him until 1991, and he knew that I was Bozo, and he knew that I was related to his father's friend. And when we first met, he asked me, Are you the one? And I said yes, and then this acquaintance turned into a friendship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 36 in line 8, it says Vuko Bajagic, Radovan's father. It must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what we have in the record now is Vuko Bajagic. It has to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So these are all just family, friendly visits with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Mostly, mostly. They were friendly family visits. There were some private calls on him at his home, I don't know if that's recorded anywhere, whether the 18 visits that year include those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: When you say "mostly," sir, does that mean that there were some business meetings, as well, or it's all just friendly meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: There were some official talks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That was my previous question, sir. What is a clerk from the Drina Corps logistics section doing meeting the president on business?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That had nothing to do with the army. I mentioned before, it had to do with some civilian issues regarding our municipality, our area, humanitarian aid, accommodation of refugees, this sentiment among the people, the talks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In what capacity were you meeting him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you see when our chief, the president of the municipality, needed to see Radovan officially, he would always ask me, saying, Zvonko, please, can you come with me? You know when you are with me, it's easier to get through. There's always a long line of people. I get to see Radovan more easily when you are with me. But it's all based on that friendship and mutual respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So who was there when you met with the president on business?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, whoever I went with. Sometimes I would leave them there to talk. I would go out. I have a relative at Pale. I would go and visit that relative, have coffee with him, until they are finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And who was the president of the municipality who you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica, three of them changed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Maybe even four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: At first, it was Milorad Lukic. He was the first one. Wait a minute. Then there was Vojo Mitrovic, that's two; Milan Gostanic [phoen], three; and afterwards, it was Dr. -- what is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Rajko Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Rajko Djukic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Rajko Djukic, no. No. You mean Rajko Dukic? There was no Djukic, D-j-u. I don't even know a Djukic. There was Ostoja Dragutinovic, I now remember, Ostoja Dragutinovic, but that was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Who is Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Director of the bauxite company in Milici, but that's another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn to a different area now, and that's your meetings with Mr. Pandurevic's Defence team. When did you first speak with someone from Mr. Pandurevic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The first I heard from them was when I got a telephone call from a lawyer by the name of Rubes in early December 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, did you know Mr. Rubes from during the war when you were a member of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What was his position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know about his position, but he was -- I think he was in the command of the Drina Corps. He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He was an administrator in the Drina Corps legal department, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So the first contact you had was a telephone call from Mr. Rubes in December 2007. Tell us about that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: He called me on the phone and asked me if he could drop by together with a lawyer from the Defence team of General Pandurevic. They [as interpreted] wanted to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did they say what they wanted to talk --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I said okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did they tell you what they wanted to talk with you about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Not on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So when did you meet with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was misinterpreted a moment ago when the witness said that he talked on the phone when Rubes called. The interpretation seems to imply that they talked on the phone in plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did the witness say according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that the investigator, lawyer Rubes, called him, saying that a defence lawyer wanted to speak to him. And then the Prosecution asked, What did they talk to you about, whereas the witness had said that Rubes spoke to him alone, not two people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Is that clear in your mind, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, then. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, after this telephone conversation with Mr. Rubes, you then met with people from General Pandurevic's Defence team; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Who was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Lawyer Rubes and lawyer Djordje and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at line 20, Mr. Mitchell, you see that your question doesn't show up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, if you could kindly repeat it, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you, who was present at that meeting? And you answered: "Lawyer Rubes and lawyer Djordje and myself." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sarapa taking notes during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: When they came, Sarapa asked me about the dinner I had prepared in Bratunac, and I told him, and I signed the record in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What precisely did he ask you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: He asked me if I remembered carrying that dinner to Bratunac. I said yes. He asked me, Do you remember when you brought that dinner? I said yes, because it had to do with the patron saint's day, which I hosted, and because I prepared meat-free food for the St. Peter's Day's fast, and the next day we ate meat. And that dinner, I brought it on the eve of St. Peter's Day on the 11th, the night of the 11th to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you didn't need any time to refresh your recollection about these -- you just remembered and told him during that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not good with dates, and I'm even worse with names. And when he said that my household said that -- had more than 172 godchildren, baptised godchildren, I had difficulty believing that. But when church holidays are concerned and church dates, I remember all that perfectly. That's why this is etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever spoken to Vinko Pandurevic about this dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What about Milenko Jevdjevic? Have you spoken with him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How many times in total have you met with a representative from Mr. Pandurevic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Later in April, Rubes called on me, but that was the next year, 2008. And I signed that record, and the following day I went to Zvornik to have that record certified at the office of a notary public in Zvornik. That's where I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just going back to that first meeting for a moment, who first brought up the topic of the dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sarapa. He asked me if I took that dinner there. I did, and I asked, Why is this interesting? And he says, Would you testify for Vinko; he suggested you as a witness, and would you testify that you did indeed carry that dinner? And I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So Mr. Pandurevic suggested you as a witness?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That's what the lawyer told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, did you follow the trial of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You know that General Krstic also said that this meeting was on the night of the 11th, or this dinner was on the night of 11 July?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with General Krstic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't even know who his Defence are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about July 1995 now, and I'd like to go through a couple of days either side of this dinner with you and get you to briefly explain to the Court what you were doing on each of those days. So if we can start off with the day before you went to this dinner in Bratunac. Can you tell the Court what you were doing on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That day or the day before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The day before the dinner,

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I went to Loznica to buy the fish. That's in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you got an order from Colonel Acamovic on the afternoon of the dinner. Why did you go and buy the fish the day before?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Because you can't buy fish anywhere closer than Serbia. We all went to buy fish there. I mean, it needed to be fresh, and we needed a lot of it for a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Why did you buy fish?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Because I told you, this is St. Peter's Day fast that takes 14 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been explained and explained already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, you were in the Drina Corps logistics organ. You must have been aware that the VRS was involved in a major operation around the Srebrenica enclave on that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened militarily that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Which day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The day before the dinner. We're still talking about the same day.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The day before the dinner.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I went to Loznica to buy the fish. Then I was at home cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Had Srebrenica fallen on the day that you went to buy the fish?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Colonel Acamovic told me when he called me in the afternoon of the 11th around 5.00 p.m. He was the first who told me that our army had entered Srebrenica. That's the first I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did he tell you that they had taken over the entire enclave?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. He just said that the army had entered Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you already had the fish by the time the VRS entered Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I bought the fish on the 10th, and I heard the news towards the evening on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the day of the dinner. What did you do that day, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the preparations for that dinner, that meat-free dinner, had started, and I had guests at my home, and this lean dinner was served at my home. And at the same time, we were roasting suckling pigs and lamb for the next day. That's what we were doing on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, this was a massive logistical operation around Srebrenica, and you're on the logistics organ. How is it that you are at home in the middle of all this, cooking food?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How is this possible?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: What have I got to do with the operation? I'm not a soldier in the battle-field. I just went to buy supplies. Whenever I had orders, I went to pick up the goods wherever and bring them to the depot of the corps, and especially on the 12th. I don't know if you understood it, but I said that I was a sponsor of the church, the sponsor of the luncheon, and the host at this celebration of St. Peter's Day for Vlasenica. I had over 1.000 guests the next day for the luncheon at the hotel, not at my home. Vasilije Kacevanola was the guest of honour to break the cake with us as the custom requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. What time did you leave Vlasenica to go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Around half past 8.00 is the time when I left to bring the food. I told Acamovic I couldn't do it any earlier. He asked me when I could do and I said, Lazar, I'm sorry. I can't do it before half past 8.00. I have things to do. And he said, Okay, do it when you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What type of car did you drive?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: A Golf. My own Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you remember the registration plates?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you put any fuel in the car before you left?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: No. The car was full, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Was anyone with you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
utterances.text: My older son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What about Zoran Sekulic? Was he with you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO BAJAGIC
